results.report:
New Year's Eve 2024 was dominated by U.S.-centered events, and the most heavily covered item was a diplomatic-style exchange rather than a conflict. The top event by article count was "SAINT consults with LOS ANGELES," with 240 articles and a mildly positive Goldstein score of 1.9. The data gives only actor labels and no further detail, so what lies behind it can't be determined. Next came "PRESIDENT consults with JUDGE" at the White House in Washington, D.C., with 104 articles (Goldstein 2.8). Together they made up the cooperative, consultative side of the day's coverage.
Most of the remaining events were coercion or fighting. The largest of these was "AUTHORITIES coerces WISCONSIN" in Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, at 70 articles (Goldstein -5.0). In Washington, D.C., "PRISON assaults WASHINGTON" drew 60 articles (Goldstein -9.0). California was a cluster: coercion events involving the United States or authorities were recorded in Palo Alto (56 articles, -9.2), Santa Clara County (42 articles, -9.2), and California more broadly (36 articles, -9.2). The near-identical scores and the shared geography suggest these may be related coverage of one situation, but the data doesn't confirm a link.
The rest were conflict-coded events with smaller article counts. "PICKPOCKET fights" in Times Square, New York, drew 40 articles (Goldstein -9.5), which fits New Year's Eve crowds there. "VANCOUVER fights" in Metchosin, British Columbia, and "UNITED STATES fights NEIGHBORHOOD" across the U.S. each had 30 articles and the most negative score on the list (-10.0). Canada's single entry stands out in a list otherwise located in the United States. The event labels are automated GDELT codings, so they point to topics in the news without establishing what actually happened.

results.report:
California's 2024 conflict coverage in this sample is dominated by violence in its big urban centers. The single most-covered event was on 2024-11-01 in Los Angeles, coded as mass violence (Goldstein -10.0) with 250 articles. In San Francisco on 2024-07-24, an event involving a "CRIMINAL" actor drew 210 articles. On 2024-08-05, a Los Angeles clash involving a hospital drew 126 articles. Another assault, in Beverly Hills on 2024-12-16, drew 112 articles at -9.0.
The rest of the sample shows conflict in other settings. On 2024-01-29, a statewide event pitting students against a gang drew 100 articles. On 2024-02-07 and 2024-02-08, fighting involving Marine Corps and San Diego actors was reported in San Diego, with 90 articles each day. On 2024-07-29, an event coded as Canada vs. United States, located only as "California," drew 96 articles. The coding of that event is ambiguous, and the data does not say what it concerned.
The one distinctly non-violent cluster is a pair of protest events in Hollywood on 2024-09-09 and 2024-09-10, involving actors and television (100 and 110 articles, Goldstein -6.5). That is milder than the -10.0 fighting events, and it points to labor or industry-related tension rather than physical confrontation, though the data does not specify the cause.
This is only a sample of the most-covered events, so it cannot show how much conflict occurred overall or how it changed during the year. It does show that Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego and Hollywood drew the heaviest coverage. Many of the actor labels are generic or machine-coded (e.g., "LOS ANGELES vs ?"), so the underlying incidents should be confirmed against the source articles.

results.query: find news articles about the Uvalde school shooting response
results.report:
The sample for 2024 is narrow. The ten most-covered events listed all fall on September 12 and 13, 2024, and all are located in Texas, mostly in Uvalde. The data says nothing about the rest of the year, so this is a snapshot of two days rather than a year in review.
The Uvalde events center on a school. On both dates, GDELT records a "GUNMAN fights SCHOOL" event in Uvalde at the most severe conflict score (Goldstein -10.0), with 70 articles on September 13 and 40 on September 12. Alongside it are consultation events involving the school, scored mildly positive (Goldstein 1.9 and 2.8) and carrying the same article counts: 70 on September 13 and 40 on September 12. Together these suggest coverage that mixed violence with discussion and engagement around the school. The data does not say what prompted the coverage.
A second thread involves Texas state actors. "TEXAS makes a public statement about TROOPER" appears on both dates (70 articles on September 13, 40 on September 12) with a neutral score of 0.0. On September 13 there is also a "TEXAS criticizes BORDER PATROL" disapproval event (Goldstein -2.0, 40 articles). The Uvalde and trooper events share the same article counts on each date, so they may come from the same coverage. The data does not confirm a link between the trooper statements, the Border Patrol criticism and the school events, and I won't assume one.

results.report:
The most heavily covered conflict events in North America in 2024 were mostly tied to U.S. political and legal disputes rather than clear-cut armed violence. Of the ten events listed, seven were in North Carolina, two in North Dakota and one in Northbrook, Illinois. This is a sample of the top events by article count, so it shows where coverage clustered, not the full scope of conflict.
North Carolina's institutions and politics dominate the list. The most-covered event was on 2024-03-13, when the COURT OF APPEALS and VOTER were coded in a "Fighting" event (70 articles, Goldstein -10.0). On 2024-10-03, PRESIDENT vs NORTH CAROLINA was coded as a show of force (63 articles, -7.2). A 2024-11-02 protest involving PRESIDENT and CHARLOTTE drew 42 articles (-6.5). Other North Carolina events include an unidentified actor against the SENATE on 2024-12-17 (60 articles, -9.5), an unidentified actor against CHARLOTTE on 2024-07-25 (56 articles, -10.0), POLICE on 2024-11-27 (50 articles, -10.0), and ACADEMICS vs LAWMAKER on 2024-09-16 (40 articles, -10.0). The actors are mostly courts, legislators, voters and city or state entities, which suggests contention over governance, elections and policing. The data does not say what each event involved, and GDELT's "Fighting" label can cover verbal or legal confrontation as well as physical clashes.
Outside North Carolina, two mirrored records from 2024-11-22 in North Dakota, NORTH DAKOTA vs JUDGE and JUDGE vs NORTH DAKOTA, each drew 50 articles at -10.0. They are most likely the same story coded from both directions, a state-versus-judiciary dispute. The remaining event is EUROPE coded in "Fighting" in Northbrook, Illinois, on 2024-04-02 (40 articles, -10.0). The actor-location pairing is odd, so it may reflect a coding quirk or a story with international links.
Overall, the sampled events point to institutional and political conflict, especially in North Carolina, as the most heavily covered form of conflict in the data. The records give no casualty or incident details, and no period comparison is provided, so they cannot show whether conflict intensified or eased over the year.

results.report:
The most heavily covered events of 2024 in this sample all center on wildfire and its fallout in the United States, with a geographic focus on Texas, Hawaii, and the West Coast. The actor labels (FIREFIGHTER, TANKER, RESIDENTS, XCEL ENERGY) point to emergency response, utilities, and affected communities. GDELT codes these as "fighting" and "appeal" events, so the "fighting" entries are probably firefighting reports rather than armed conflict.
In Texas, the biggest cluster falls in late winter. On February 29, an unidentified actor made a public statement about COMMUNITY (102 articles). On March 3, two mirrored "fighting" events pairing FIREFIGHTER and TEXAS each drew 64 articles at the maximum conflict score of -10.0. On March 7, a public statement about XCEL ENERGY drew 70 articles, which suggests the utility was drawn into the story. The data does not say what the statement concerned.
In the summer, attention moved west. On July 27, OREGON made a public statement about TANKER (60 articles). On July 29, an unidentified actor criticized CALIFORNIA in Butte County (60 articles, Goldstein -2.0). On August 4 in Hawaii, RESIDENTS were tied to a fighting event (60 articles, -9.5), and a SCHOOL expressed intent to cooperate (60 articles, +4.0). Hawaii returned on September 13 with the two most heavily covered events in the sample: TANKER appealing to FIREFIGHTER (105 articles) and RESIDENTS in a fighting event (100 articles, -10.0).
Taken together, the sample shows a year in which fire emergencies in several states generated sustained coverage. Conflict-coded firefighting and resident events sit alongside appeals, public statements, and offers of cooperation. This is only a top-10 sample, so it shows which events drew the most coverage, not how often fires occurred or how the year developed. The records also give no cause, damage, or outcome for any event.

results.report:
Protest coverage in Texas during the week of December 23–29, 2024 was spread across several unrelated threads. The data is thin on detail: the event records carry actor labels and conflict scores but no narrative text, so what drove each protest is mostly unclear. The ten most-covered events in the sample each drew 8 to 10 articles, and nearly all carry the same Goldstein score of -6.5.
The week opened on December 23 with two events at 10 articles each. One pitted Starbucks against a "company" actor, which suggests a labor or corporate dispute. The other, the most severe in the sample at Goldstein -7.5, involved Texas against "deputies." On December 24, activity centered on Dallas and San Antonio. Separate San Antonio-tagged events were recorded in San Antonio and New Braunfels, each with 8 articles. A Seattle-versus-company event was also located in Texas that day, which may reflect a corporate dispute with a Seattle link rather than a Seattle-based protest.
Later in the week, a government-related protest was logged statewide on December 25. On December 27, a generic "male" actor was tied to a protest event. On December 28, a constable-related protest was recorded in Jersey Village, near Houston, alongside another statewide Texas-tagged event, each with 10 articles. The constable and deputy events suggest recurring friction involving local law enforcement, though the data doesn't say what caused it.
Overall, the sample points to scattered protests involving corporate, government and law enforcement actors rather than one dominant movement. Because many records are tagged only to "Texas" and have vague actors, the specific causes and participants can't be determined from this data alone.

April 2024 in Texas, as reflected in the most heavily covered events, was shaped by protest, conflict-coded incidents in the Houston area, and political friction. This is a sample of ten events, so it shows what drew attention rather than the full scope of the month.
The mid-month events were mostly conflict-coded. On April 12, "HOUSTON fights" appeared in two records, one in Harris County (100 articles) and one in Houston itself (80 articles), both scoring -10.0 on the Goldstein scale. The next day, April 13, an unidentified actor was recorded fighting TEXAS (105 articles, also -10.0). The data doesn't say what happened in these incidents, only that they drew substantial coverage. Earlier, on April 3, a presidential candidate was recorded criticizing an unspecified target in Texas (90 articles, Goldstein -2.0).
The month's final days were dominated by protest-related coverage. On April 27, an "ISRAEL investigates PROTESTER" event in Texas drew 128 articles, the highest count in this sample. On April 29, a student protester was recorded rejecting TEXAS (90 articles, Goldstein -5.0). Together these suggest campus and activist demonstrations tied to the Israel-related issue were a major story, though the records alone don't give the specifics. On April 28, JORDAN made a public statement about a COMPANY in Houston (105 articles, Goldstein 0.0), but the data doesn't explain the context.
Cooperative signals also appeared. On April 22, an unidentified actor consulted with "THE BELOVED COUNTRY" in Texas (80 articles, Goldstein 1.9). On April 25, two mirrored records show intent to cooperate involving the same actor (120 articles each, Goldstein 4.0). The actor label is ambiguous, so the data doesn't make clear who or what was involved.

The sample is only ten events, so it shows what drew the most attention, not the full scope of the month.

Another Houston consultation, involving an unidentified actor and "MELBOURNE" on 2024-02-08, drew 102 articles. On 2024-02-12, two events tied to Houston involved "TEXAS" and "ABBOT" and drew 90 articles each. One was coded as fighting with a Goldstein score of -10.0, the most conflictual in the set. The other was a public statement with a near-neutral -0.4. The actor labels are terse, so the data does not say what these exchanges were about. On 2024-02-29, a "JUDGE" coercing a "MIGRANT" (Goldstein -5.0) and a "LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER" yielding (Goldstein 5.0) each drew 80 articles. The same day also saw an unidentified actor make a public statement about "COMMUNITY" across Texas, with 102 articles. Earlier, on 2024-02-02, a "RADIO STATION" public statement drew 80 articles. On 2024-02-27, "JOE BIDEN" expressed intent to cooperate with the "UNITED STATES," also with 80 articles, tying the state's stories to national politics.
Taken together, the sample shows a mix of cooperative and consultative events alongside sharply conflictual ones, with the Abbott-related fighting event and the judge-migrant coercion event as the clearest friction points. **The primary event** is an appeal involving "AUTHORITIES" in Fort Worth, Texas, recorded on 2024-01-09 and covered in 120 articles. It carries a neutral Goldstein score of 3.0. The data does not say who appealed, to whom, or about what. The actor field lists only AUTHORITIES against an unknown counterpart, and one record shows the date as unknown. The event's content therefore can't be established from this data alone, and any link to the related events below is only suggested by the shared actor label and the school-related locations.
**The related events** that appear in the data cluster around schools and local authorities in early January 2024. The largest is a Fighting event (Goldstein -10.0) involving AUTHORITIES and a PUPIL in Iowa on 2024-01-06, with 100 articles. Perry High School, Iowa, appears in three records dated 2024-01-05, each with 70 articles: AUTHORITIES consulting with POLICE (2.8), POLICE fighting AUTHORITIES (-10.0), and POLICE consulting with AUTHORITIES (1.9). The mix of cooperative and conflict codes for the same location and date is typical of how GDELT codes a single incident from many angles. Separately, a Consultation event (Goldstein 1.0) took place at Robb Elementary School, Texas, on 2024-01-18, with 80 articles. That puts school-related activity in Texas as well, though the data doesn't explain it.
**Other AUTHORITIES events** in the set are less obviously connected. On 2024-01-05, AUTHORITIES threatened RESIDENTS in Maine (-4.4, 60 articles). On 2024-01-02, AUTHORITIES criticized an unnamed party in Michigan (-2.0, 60 articles). On 2024-01-31, AUTHORITIES made a public statement about MANCHESTER in New Hampshire (0.0, 60 articles). Together they show that "AUTHORITIES" is a generic actor label used across many US states, so the Fort Worth appeal can't be tied to these events on the evidence provided.
Only eight of the 50 related events were supplied, and no period comparison was included, so this summary says nothing about broader trends. The Fort Worth appeal's 120 articles make it the most heavily covered item in the set, ahead of the Iowa fighting event at 100.

The pairing of military personnel and sheriff's deputies in one county does suggest a coordinated local response of some kind.
Elsewhere, the coverage reflected a mix of cooperation and conflict. In Houston, a military aid event drew 20 articles and was the most cooperative in the sample (Goldstein 8.3). Conflict-coded events included "fighting" in Brazoria County involving North Carolina as an actor (Goldstein -10.0, 20 articles) and a migrant-versus-governor confrontation statewide (Goldstein -9.5, 20 articles). An administration coercion event (Goldstein -5.0, 24 articles) was also logged. The event records give no further detail on these, so their causes and connections are unknown.
Several statewide events involved national or international actors, tagged to Texas without a specific locale. They included a U.S. public statement about Egypt (24 articles), U.S. diplomatic cooperation (20 articles, Goldstein 3.5), and a prosecutor's public statement about Boeing (20 articles). Their Texas geotagging may reflect where the stories were reported rather than where the events happened. These records are a sample of the most-covered events, so they show what drew attention that day, not the full scope of what happened in Texas.

results.report:
Canada's November 2024 record in GDELT is large but thinly characterized by the events surfaced here. The regional summary shows 116,142 events for the period, with 16,362 coded as cooperation and 9,730 as conflict. Average tone was mildly negative at -1.32, and the average Goldstein score was slightly positive at 0.86. Taken together, the month leans toward routine, low-intensity interaction, with cooperative events outnumbering conflictual ones.
The most heavily covered events are few and carry little actor detail. On 2024-11-11, an event in Holyrood, Newfoundland, involving a "CANADIAN" actor drew 160 articles with a clearly cooperative tone (6.0). On 2024-11-15, a nationally located event involving an "INVESTOR" actor drew 140 articles, also cooperative (5.2). Neither names a counterpart, so the underlying story isn't clear from the data alone. They do suggest that community-level and economic themes were among the more widely reported items.
The sharper negative signals come from two places. On 2024-11-14 in Etobicoke, Ontario, an event involving a "HUNTER" actor drew 109 articles with a strongly conflictual tone (-10.0). On 2024-11-27 in Montreal, Quebec, two records involving a "STUDENT" actor drew 97 and 95 articles, with tones of -2.0 (neutral) and -9.0 (conflict). Their near-identical article counts suggest the same underlying story coded twice, though the data doesn't say what happened. Because the actor labels are generic and the counterparts unknown, these entries show where media attention clustered but not the causes or outcomes. Only five top events are listed here, so they are a narrow sample of a much larger month, and no comparison to a prior period is available to judge whether the overall picture shifted.

results.report:
Coverage of Mexico on December 30-31, 2024 is dominated by violence tied to organized crime, with one political protest standing out as the single most-covered event. The most-reported item in the sample was a protest involving "PRESIDENT" actors in Tlaxcala, Tlaxcala on December 30 (30 articles, Goldstein -6.5). It was milder in tone than the fighting events that make up the rest of the list.
The armed violence centers on cartel activity. On December 30, fighting between CARTEL and ARMY actors was recorded in Coalcoman, Michoacán de Ocampo (20 articles, Goldstein -10.0). Michoacán-labeled fighting involving "MEXICO" actors drew the same 20 articles that day. Fighting attributed to CRIMINAL actors in Sinaloa (20 articles) was logged on December 30, and a CARTEL-labeled fighting event in Sinaloa followed on December 31 (20 articles). The geocoding is imprecise: these records pair Sinaloa and Michoacán with "Tabasco," which suggests location-matching errors in the source data rather than a real geographic link.
Other events in the sample are smaller and harder to interpret. These include fighting between "WORKER" and "UNITED STATES" actors across Mexico on December 31 (12 articles), and fighting involving "MEXICO" and "PRIEST" actors on December 30 (10 articles). Also logged on December 30 were an assault event pairing "SOLICITOR GENERAL" and "MONK" in Juarez (10 articles), a generic CIVILIAN fighting event (10 articles), and a "HOSPITAL" fighting event in Puebla (10 articles). Several of these actor labels look like coding artifacts, so they should be read cautiously.
Taken together, the sample suggests that cartel-army clashes in Michoacán and criminal violence in Sinaloa were the main conflict stories of these two days. This is only a sample of the most-covered events, so it cannot show the overall scale of violence or any trend over time.

December 2024 protest coverage in Ohio centered on labor disputes and tensions with law enforcement, based on a sample of the ten most-covered events. Every event in the sample drew 10 articles and carried a conflict tone, with Goldstein scores of -6.5 or -7.5. The data is thin on detail: most events are statewide ("Ohio, United States") with generic actor labels, so the specifics behind each protest are not clear from the records.
Worker-related actions were the most visible thread. On December 22, a WORKER vs UNITED STATES protest was logged in Ohio. On December 30, workers were recorded protesting against PITTSBURGH in Lordstown, a location tied to Ohio's manufacturing sector. On December 20, a TOLEDO vs WORKER event appeared. The actor labels alone don't reveal the employers or issues involved, so any link between these events is only suggested by the shared actor category.
Policing drew the sharpest tone. Two events scored -7.5, the most negative in the sample: OHIO vs POLICE on December 5, and a POLICE-related protest in Dayton on December 14. A DEPUTIES protest was also logged on December 5. The remaining events involved community and institutional voices: MEDIA protests on December 2 and 6, a COMMUNITY protest on December 3, and a YWCA protest on December 17. The records do not say what prompted them. Taken together, the sample shows a month of protest activity in Ohio spanning labor, public safety and civic organizations, though the sparse event descriptions limit firmer conclusions.

results.query: protests in New York in September 2024
results.report:
September 2024 in New York opened with protest at Columbia University. On September 4, an event pitting police against demonstrators drew 16 articles, with a Goldstein score of -7.5, the most conflictual in this sample. A separate September 4 event, police protests against New York, drew 16 articles at -6.5. Both fit the academic year's return to campus, though the data doesn't say what prompted either event.
The coverage then turns to labor and civic actors. Protests involving "president" (September 5), "worker" (September 11) and "company" (September 25) each drew 20 articles, the highest count in this sample. The data names no specific grievances, employers or demands. A related September 13 event, an employer-versus-worker protest, was recorded in New Hampshire (12 articles), so it falls outside New York itself.
Around September 20, two events (New York against "activist," and activists on their own) also drew 20 articles each. On September 23, Columbus Circle was the site of two events tied to the Israel–Gaza conflict, one listing the United States against Israel and the other Gaza against Israel, each with 16 articles. The timing matches the diplomatic activity in the city that week, but the data doesn't confirm a link.
Every event in this sample is coded as Protest with conflict tone, at -6.5 or -7.5. Many actor labels are generic ("worker," "company," "activist"), so the data shows the themes of the month (campus policing, labor, and Middle East-related demonstrations) but not who organized them or how they ended.

results.report:
Arizona's February 2024 GDELT record contains 20,942 events. Of these, 1,947 are coded as conflict and 2,599 as cooperation. The average Goldstein score is about +0.42, slightly cooperative, and the average tone is about -2.28, mildly negative. Most coverage sits in the neutral middle, with cooperation outnumbering conflict only modestly.
The most heavily covered events come from a small set. On 2024-02-01 in Phoenix, two mirrored records, "PREMIER vs PHOENIX" and "PHOENIX vs PREMIER", each drew 80 articles with a neutral tone (4.0). The identical actors and article counts suggest one underlying story recorded twice. The actor labels are ambiguous, so the data doesn't show whether this is a sports, business or political item. It may well be a sports matchup, but that is an inference.
Later in the month, three statewide records with unresolved counterparts stand out. On 2024-02-23, "ADMINISTRATION vs ?" drew 60 articles with a cooperative tone (7.0). On 2024-02-24, "GOVERNOR vs ?" drew 80 articles with a neutral tone (3.0). On 2024-02-25, "ARIZONA vs ?" drew 80 articles with a slightly negative tone (-2.0). These records are tied to the state as a whole rather than a city, and the sequence suggests government activity in the final week. But the actor fields are generic and the second party is missing, so the data can't show what policy, decision or incident was involved.
The picture is limited. The top events are only a sample ranked by article count, with vague actor coding, so they can't establish themes or trends. The summary figures show a broadly stable, mildly cooperative environment with a negative media tone, but explaining the drivers would require the underlying articles.

results.report:
The most-covered protest events in the data that are actually located in Washington, DC, center largely on the Gaza war and its political fallout. The top DC-tagged event is dated 2024-05-01 and was coded as "California protests against Hamas." It drew 70 articles, the most of any event listed. Other DC events point the same way: a 2024-01-13 event coded "Washington vs Gaza" (40 articles) and a 2024-08-23 event coded "Intelligence vs Israel" (48 articles). The actor labels are automated GDELT codings, so they show the themes of coverage but not who was actually protesting.
Several events cluster around domestic politics and policing. On 2024-07-15, an event coded "Washington vs Lawmaker" drew 32 articles. On 2024-07-26, two separate DC events each drew 50 articles: one coded "Protester vs Law Enforcement Agencies" and one coded "Unidentified actor vs Male." The shared date and location suggest they may describe the same episode, but the data doesn't confirm that. A 2024-05-23 event coded only as "Hunter" (30 articles) is too thin to interpret.
Some of the top "Washington" events are not in DC at all. The 2024-04-23 event (Palestine vs Jewish, 50 articles) is placed in Morningside, Washington State. Three others come from Washington State: Seattle on 2024-09-13 (Aerospace vs Boeing, 50 articles), a 2024-10-24 Boeing protest (50 articles), and Morningside. These appear to reflect labor and corporate disputes and shouldn't be counted as DC activity.
The DC picture is a sample of high-coverage events, not a full record of the year. It shows that Gaza-related demonstrations and confrontations with authorities drew the most media attention in the capital, and it doesn't say how often protests occurred or whether they grew or declined.

results.report:
Canada dominates the most-covered protest events in this 2024 sample, with demonstrations spread across the country's major cities. The single most-covered event was in Toronto on April 6, where protesters clashed with police (78 articles, Goldstein -7.5). Toronto returned to the coverage on April 8 with another protester-versus-police confrontation (46 articles, -7.5), and on January 11, when demonstrators targeted the city itself (49 articles).
Quebec supplied the next-largest cluster. Montreal appears three times: February 29, an event with CANADA as the actor (60 articles); January 16, a civilian-led protest against an actor identified as KINGSTON (50 articles); and May 12, a police-versus-protester event (50 articles, -7.5). In Quebec City on July 17, a protest involving a producer drew 58 articles. The data doesn't say what drove these events, so the underlying grievances can't be read from the actor labels alone.
Labor and government-facing protests appear elsewhere. On February 12 in Ottawa, nurses protested against Ontario (54 articles). On May 10 in Winnipeg, an unidentified actor protested against Manitoba (50 articles). On December 17 in Vancouver, an employee protest against Canada drew 48 articles. Most of these events carry a Goldstein score of -6.5, and the two police-versus-protester confrontations in Toronto and Montreal register the sharpest conflict at -7.5.
This is only a sample of the ten most-covered events, so it shows where coverage concentrated, not how much protest activity occurred overall or how it changed over the year. It points to Toronto and Montreal as the main flashpoints, with police confrontations drawing the most intense conflict ratings.

results.query: Were there more protests in Texas in October than in September?
results.report:
Protest activity in Texas picked up markedly from September to October 2024. The comparison's verdict reads: "October 2024 is up 62.3% per day versus September 2024 (248 to 416 events)." That puts September at 248 events over 30 days (8.27 per day, 2024-09-01 to 2024-09-30), and October at 416 events over 31 days (13.42 per day, 2024-10-01 to 2024-10-31).
The two months are not the same length, 30 days versus 31, so the comparison is based on events per day rather than raw totals. The change in events per day is +62.3%. Because the per-day figure already accounts for the extra day in October, the rise is not an artifact of a longer month.
The data here covers only the comparison counts, filtered to location=Texas and event_type=protest. It includes no individual events, actors, cities, or article counts, so it shows how much protest activity rose but not what drove it. Explaining the cause would require looking at the specific events within each month.

plan.thinking: The question compares two periods, so I count every matching event in September 2024 and October 2024 and compute the change deterministically instead of summarising a sample.
plan.report_prompt: Explain this period comparison for protest events in Texas. Quote the verdict and the counts exactly as given and do not recompute them.

data.verdict: October 2024 is up 62.3% per day versus September 2024 (248 to 416 events).
caveats: Periods have different lengths (30 vs 31 days); direction is based on events per day.

results.query: Did conflict events in Mexico go down this month?
results.report:
**Conflict reporting in Mexico held essentially steady from November to December 2024.** The comparison's verdict reads: "About flat: 7,829 events in November 2024 vs 8,008 in this month (-1.0% per day)." November (2024-11-01 to 2024-11-30) logged 7,829 conflict events over 30 days, or 260.97 per day. The following period (2024-12-01 to 2024-12-31) logged 8,008 events over 31 days, or 258.32 per day.
The raw totals and the daily rates seem to point in different directions, and the periods' lengths explain why. December's total is higher than November's, but it also covers 31 days against November's 30. The caveat in the data says so directly: "Periods have different lengths (30 vs 31 days); direction is based on events per day." On that per-day basis, the change is -1.0%, a marginal dip rather than a rise.
The takeaway is stability. Under the filters used (location=Mexico, event_type=conflict), the daily volume of recorded conflict events barely moved between the two months. The data supplies no breakdown by actor, region, or event type, so it cannot show what drove the activity in either month or whether the makeup of events shifted beneath the flat headline.

results.query: How did protest activity in Canada change from Q1 to Q2?
results.report:
Protest activity in Canada held roughly steady across the first half of 2024. The comparison verdict reads "About flat: 2,799 events in Q1 2024 vs 2,912 in Q2 2024 (+4.0% per day)." Both quarters span the same 91 days, so the two periods line up directly.
In Q1 2024 (2024-01-01 to 2024-03-31), the data records 2,799 protest events, or 30.76 per day. In Q2 2024 (2024-04-01 to 2024-06-30), it records 2,912 events, or 32.0 per day. The change in events per day is +4.0%, which the verdict labels as essentially flat rather than a meaningful shift.
The takeaway is one of continuity. Canada's protest event volume in the second quarter stayed very close to the first quarter's level, and the small difference in the daily rate does not point to a clear escalation or decline. The data supplied covers only these two period totals, filtered to location=Canada and event_type=protest. It includes no breakdown by issue, region, or actor, so it cannot say what drove the protests in either quarter.

Florida's 2024 record in this dataset is dominated by a cluster of mid-December events. On December 17, three separate items each drew 250 articles: a federal judge's public statement involving the District of Columbia (Goldstein -2.0), and two consultations involving Congress (Goldstein 1.9 and 2.8). Another December 17 event, a lawyer appealing to China, drew 220 articles, and on December 18 an unidentified actor expressed intent to cooperate with Joe Biden (150 articles). The data gives only actors and event types, not the substance of these exchanges. The overlap in dates and in the Florida location suggests a single news cycle involving federal institutions, but the records alone don't establish what it was.
Earlier in the year, the most-covered activity centered on Escambia County. On July 24, a school-related public statement drew 220 articles, and a coercion event attributed to "Florida" drew 176 articles at a sharply negative Goldstein score of -5.0. These two events share a date and county, which points to a connected development involving a school and state action, though the data doesn't say what it was. On August 5, an event coded as Florida threatening Florida (Goldstein -4.4, 150 articles) pointed to internal tension within the state, again without detail on its cause.
The remaining entries are more cooperative in tone. On March 12, Miami and a school engaged in diplomatic cooperation, the most positive event in the sample (Goldstein 8.0, 150 articles). On October 19, Arkansas was coded as consulting in Florida (Goldstein 2.8, 150 articles). Taken together, these top events mix conflict-coded items (coercion, threats, a judicial statement) with consultation and cooperation. Because they are a sample ranked by article count and the coded actors are often generic, they show what drew the most coverage rather than a full account of the year in Florida.

Texas protest coverage in 2024, as captured by the most-covered events in this sample, centers on a cluster of demonstrations in Austin on April 24. Four of the ten events share that date: AUSTIN vs TROOPER (40 articles), PALESTINE vs AUSTIN (40 articles), PALESTINE vs POLICE (30 articles), and AUSTIN vs TEXAS (30 articles). The actor pairings suggest pro-Palestinian demonstrators confronting law enforcement, including state troopers. Each event carries a conflict tone of -6.5 on the Goldstein scale. A related event on April 30, DEMONSTRATOR vs POLICE (30 articles), points to continued friction with police later that month.
Other episodes show that the year's unrest was not confined to a single issue. On February 2, a protest involving TEXAS drew 30 articles in Eagle Pass, a border community. The data does not specify the cause, but the location is notable. On February 26, a WASHINGTON vs ISRAELI protest registered 30 articles and the sharpest tone in the sample (Goldstein -7.5), which ties Texas coverage to the Israel-Gaza issue. An April 6 protest listed under UNITED STATES drew 36 articles, though the actors are not specified.
Later in the year, the sample includes a May 30 event pitting STUDENT against TEXAS (40 articles), which fits with campus-related activism. On July 25, an INDUSTRY protest drew 30 articles, with no further detail on its subject.
Taken together, these records suggest that Gaza-related activism, campus and student mobilization, and clashes with police were prominent threads in Texas protest coverage, with Austin as a focal point. The data is only a sample of the most-covered events and gives limited detail on causes, participants, or outcomes, so these links are inferences from actor labels and dates rather than confirmed findings.

results.query: news about the Baltimore bridge collapse
results.report:
The most-covered events in this 2024 sample are concentrated in Maryland. The single most-covered item is a March 28 "yield" involving police in Maryland, with 100 articles. Two more Maryland events share that date. A worker making a public statement about Honduras drew 70 articles. Another set of events falls in the days just before and after it: March 27 (New York), March 29 (New York) and March 31 and April 1 (Baltimore). The data does not name the underlying incident, but the actors (engineer, worker, a British actor, a regulator, a company) and the Baltimore setting suggest one major story with several angles.
Within that cluster, the tones vary. On April 1, an engineer made a public statement in Baltimore (63 articles). On March 31, a "BRITISH fights UNITED STATES" event in Baltimore was the most conflictual item in the sample (Goldstein -10.0, 48 articles). An immigrant-related appeal in Maryland the same day was mildly positive (+3.0, 46 articles). In New York, a company threatened a regulator on March 29 (-7.0, 50 articles). On March 27, a "Maryland yields to population" event scored the most cooperative value in the sample (+10.0, 44 articles).
The autumn events form a separate thread. On September 18, an immigrant-related investigation of the United States was logged in Washington, D.C. (-2.0, 50 articles). Three days later, on September 21, a criminal investigation in Maryland drew 80 articles (-2.0). On October 25, a deputy yielded to a settlement in Maryland (+7.0, 80 articles), one of the more cooperative events in the sample.
This is only a sample of the ten most-covered events, so it shows what drew heavy coverage, not how events were distributed or how activity changed over the year. Maryland dominates the list. The data supports a cluster of coverage tied to Baltimore around late March and early April, but not the cause or full scope of that story.

results.query: search for articles mentioning hurricane Helene
results.report:
The most heavily covered events in this sample cluster in the southeastern United States between late September and early October 2024, centered on North Carolina and Florida. The pattern is consistent with the aftermath of a major hurricane season, though the data doesn't name a specific storm or cause, so that link is inference rather than something the records state.
The earliest events were in Florida. On 2024-09-26, Mexico consulted with Florida (64 articles), followed on 2024-09-27 by Florida consulting with an unidentified party (65 articles). On 2024-09-28, Atlanta was recorded providing aid in Florida (78 articles, Goldstein 7.4), the most cooperative event in the sample. The same day, Tennessee criticized (72 articles, Goldstein -2.0) and made a public statement in North Carolina (70 articles, Goldstein -0.4). On 2024-09-29, an unidentified actor threatened North Carolina (70 articles, Goldstein -4.4), the most negative event listed.
The densest coverage came on 2024-10-02 in North Carolina. A public statement by North Carolina drew 93 articles, the highest count in the sample. Two consultation events involving the President each drew 86 articles (Goldstein 2.8 and 1.9). On 2024-10-08, Washington expressed intent to cooperate with Germany, located in Tampa Bay, Florida (70 articles, Goldstein 4.0).
Taken together, the sample shows state-level statements, aid and consultations in Florida and North Carolina, with a presidential role in the North Carolina coverage. The data covers only ten events, all from a roughly two-week window, so it says nothing about the rest of 2024. The actor labels are also coarse. Places such as Atlanta and Tennessee appear as actors, and several counterparts are unidentified.
